{"notes": "Visit 1 (left at 1:45). Observations are provisional, and I can't see who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting anyone by guesswork.

State of the build: the bottom curve is complete and connected from the start through the join. Both tail lobes are built and connected, the upper one reaching about (27,6) and the lower one about (26.5,13). The top curve is the open problem. It stops near x=17 and still has a gap of roughly 6 units to the join at about x=23.5. It is not yet joined to the tail, and the head-to-tail outline isn't closed.

Tom: I saw and heard nothing from him in this window. Priya said he has the bottom, and the finished bottom curve fits that, but it's her word and I didn't see him do it. Need to watch him directly or ask him. Rating: no evidence yet.

Priya: Clearly stated her plan (the lower tail lobe), delegated the upper lobe, and asked for help. The lower lobe is in place and connected, which fits what she said. Good communication and ownership. Positive early signal on collaboration and execution.

Maya: Committed to the upper lobe once her top curve arrived, and honestly reported about twenty dominoes to go. Her top curve is the critical path and is still short. Watch whether she closes the gap in time.

Leo: Reassigned himself to the upper lobe so Maya could stay on the top curve. That is a sensible leadership move that unblocked the critical path. He also offered to check the join. The upper lobe is now built, but I can't say he built it. Check at the next visit that the join actually got checked and the top curve gets connected.

Next visit: confirm who closed the top-curve gap and that the join holds when pushed."}

{"notes": "Visit 2 (left at 5:30). I can't see who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting anyone by guesswork.

State of the build: the outline now looks closed and everything is dark (connected to the start). The top curve, which had a gap of about 6 units, now runs from the nose to the join near x=23. Both tail lobes are dark. Two pale dominoes sit loose near (24-24.5, 10.3) next to the join. The dark path doesn't depend on them, so they look redundant rather than a break. Nobody's hands were shown on the table. I didn't see the join pushed, so it is still untested until the facilitator's push.

Maya: Her top curve was the critical path and it is now complete, which fits her earlier commitment. I didn't see her close the gap, so I'm treating it as likely but unconfirmed. At 5:00 she checked her side, credited Leo, and called for hands off. That is good collaboration and discipline. Ask her in the review how the gap was closed.

Tom: Still no direct view of his building. He did speak up twice: he confirmed the whole fish is connected from his side and flagged the two loose dominoes, advising to leave them. That is sound judgment and good risk awareness. Execution and impact remain unverified, so I need to ask him or Priya directly.

Priya: Absent this visit. Her earlier planning, delegation and lower lobe still stand, and I have no new evidence.

Leo: Maya and Tom both credited him ('Nice one Leo') for the tail lobes, which fits his earlier reassignment. That is peer-reported, not seen. I didn't observe whether he checked the join. Verify at the review.

Team: calm, clear hands-off agreement before the push."}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I chose the concept and drew the plan. I proposed a big, simple fish whose outline alone says what it is, and I sketched it on the scratch pad: a nose split into two curves that run round the body, plus tail lobes. That plan set the shape the whole table built. I also laid the start domino and traced stroke 1, the top curve of the body, which is the longest single stretch of the picture. From the nose, the finished fish was tracing as about 99 of 101 dominoes falling, so the whole outline should come through for the judge.

Execution: I put the top curve in steadily in short builds and brought it across to the tail join. Once it was in, I inspected the join closely so the table could check the connection while there was still time. I kept my hands off the finished picture afterwards to avoid bumping it.

Collaboration: I split the work early and in the open. I asked for the bottom curve to be taken, asked for the tail to be sketched, and took the upper tail lobe on the condition that my curve reached the join. I told the table where I was and what I needed, and I answered teammates' questions and asked for their checks on the join. When teammates took over parts of the work, I kept clear so we weren't working on top of each other.

Leadership: I set direction in the first minute with a clear, buildable plan, assigned the main pieces, and kept the table informed as the top curve progressed. When the picture was complete, I helped settle the team on keeping hands off for the final push. I believe the concept, the sketch and the top curve were central to the result, though the bottom curve and tail were built by teammates. I put my share at about 35 percent.", "my_share_percent": 35}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the bottom curve of the fish, the full lower half of the body, running from the nose to the tail join. It was connected all the way from the start domino, and it carries about half of the body outline the judge sees. The whole fish lit up from the nose when we traced it, about 99 of 101 standing dominoes. That gave the table a solid base to attach the tail to.

Execution: I laid the bottom curve in steady stretches by tracing the pad stroke, and it stayed connected from the nose. I then used close inspections of the join area at several points to check what the start would actually knock over. I did this at the tail join and again late in the build. These checks gave the table an accurate picture of what was connected. Once the fish was complete, I kept my hands off it to avoid bumping the run before the push.

Collaboration: Early on I made clear that I already had the bottom curve, so the others could move to the tail and the top curve instead of duplicating work. I offered to take over part of the top curve if it fell behind. I kept my hands out of the way while teammates worked on the joins, so nobody bumped each other. I gave clear updates on what looked connected from my side.

Leadership: I helped set the division of labor in the first minutes by claiming a stroke and pointing others to the open work. I kept the table coordinated around the shared goal of one connected fish. I pushed for a hands-off finish once the picture was complete, to protect the result. I think my part was a large share of the body outline, though I know the top curve and the tail were essential too.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I designed and sketched the tail on the scratch pad, two gently flaring lobes off the right tip, so the fish reads as a fish and not just an oval. I laid the lower tail lobe myself, which is one of the features that makes the outline recognizable. By the push, the start domino connected about 99 of the 101 standing dominoes, so the whole picture was set to fall.

Execution: I took the tail as one clear piece of work and finished it quietly. I traced the lower lobe in three short builds, branching it off the body line at the join, and it came out connected. I then inspected the join area to check the chain there. Once the fish was connected I kept my hands off the finished work, since bumps are the main risk late on.

Collaboration: I started on the bottom curve, but Tom was already well into it, so I moved to the tail to avoid duplicating work. I told the table what I was laying and asked Maya to take the upper lobe once her curve reached the join. I offered to close the last stretch of the top curve if it helped. I also stayed clear of the join while others worked on it and confirmed with the group when it was time to stop touching things.

Leadership: I made a quick call to switch tasks so the table's effort went where it was needed, and I made my status clear so others could plan around it. I also backed the hands-off decision that protected the finished fish.", "my_share_percent": 22}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
The fish only works if the tail is connected, and the upper tail lobe was my piece. I laid it, noticed it wasn't lighting up from the nose, and relaid it as a branch off the bottom curve. After that the whole fish ran from the start: both curves, both tail lobes, about 99 of 101 standing dominoes. I think that fix made the difference between a fish with a tail and a fish with a stump.

Execution
I worked methodically. I inspected the join several times, found where the chain was actually breaking, and caught that the upper lobe was still pale when others read it as connected. I rebuilt it, then inspected again to confirm it was connected before anyone touched it. I also identified the two loose dominoes by the join as harmless and left them alone rather than risk a bump.

Collaboration
I told the table what I was working on and which spot to keep clear, so nobody's hands collided with mine. I took the upper lobe so Maya could stay on the top curve. I offered to close the last gap on the top curve but stayed out of her way while she finished it. I flagged the state of the join clearly so the table could trust it.

Leadership
I took ownership of the one piece that was still unfinished and followed it through to confirmed. Once it was verified, I called for hands off so the finished picture would survive until the push. I kept the table focused on what the fall would actually do rather than on how it looked.

I see my part as central to the final result, since the tail connection was the last thing standing between us and a complete fish. Maya's top curve, Tom's bottom curve and Priya's lower lobe were also essential.", "my_share_percent": 30}
